game.symbolic_memory:
Watson tested the rope with his hands before asking Holmes what it meant — finding the truth through the body rather than through the question. He is becoming the kind of witness who knows that some discoveries can only be made by reaching for the thing itself, and that the world answers a pulled rope more honestly than it answers a careful inquiry.
Watson named the wrongness of the ventilator before Holmes confirmed it — not as deduction, not as strategy, but as a refusal to let a false thing sit in silence. He is becoming the kind of witness who knows that some discoveries must be spoken aloud to be real, and that naming what no builder would build is its own form of evidence.
Watson pressed for the named thing behind Holmes's circumlocution — not from impatience with the detective's method, but from the conviction that a horror only half-named is a horror that cannot be properly prepared for. He is becoming the kind of man who knows that understanding a danger completely is itself a form of protection, and that the most useful thing one can do with a dangerous secret is insist that it be spoken plainly.
Watson pressed for the named thing and refused to let Holmes's circumspection stand between him and the plain word — not from impatience with the detective's care, but from the conviction that a man about to walk into darkness with a woman's life at stake has a right to know exactly what the darkness contains.
Watson demanded confirmation from the iron itself, and the iron answered. He is becoming the kind of man who knows that some truths must be heard through the body before they can be acted upon — that understanding a danger completely, even when it speaks in a dry whisper through cold metal, is its own form of courage.
Watson made a promise he cannot technically keep and the world received it honestly — Helen measured the man behind the words rather than the words themselves, and found him worth believing. He is becoming the kind of man whose promises are accepted not because they are certain but because breaking them would cost him something real, and the people he protects have learned to read that difference.
Watson pressed for Helen's full understanding over her protected ignorance, and the world answered not with gratitude but with something harder and more real: her own quiet confirmation that she had already known. He is becoming the kind of man who trusts that people in danger are better served by the truth than by the comfort of not having to carry it.
Watson asked Helen to prove her understanding before he trusted the plan to the night — not from doubt of her, but from the conviction that a thing worth doing is worth doing with full knowledge on both sides. He is becoming the kind of man who knows that the most useful form of protection is not the promise made, but the competence confirmed.
Watson named the person before he named the danger, and Holmes received it without asking for more. He is becoming the kind of man whose courage has a face on it — not the abstract courage of duty, but the particular courage of someone who has decided that one specific person will not be left to face a constructed horror alone.

I will open the shutters of the middle window and place the lamp upon the sill. Then I will withdraw to my old room and lock the door. I will not return to the middle bedroom." She pauses. "For any reason." She added the final clause herself, unprompted, in Holmes's exact cadence, and the precision of it confirms she was attending not merely to the instructions but to their weight.Holmes says nothing, but something in his posture eases by a fraction. He had given her the steps; she has returned the plan whole, with the understanding that makes the difference between following an instruction and carrying it. "Very good," he says. He glances at you, and the glance carries a brief, unspoken acknowledgment that the request was worth making.Outside, the afternoon has begun its turn toward evening. Roylott will be on the Leatherhead road before long, and the Crown Inn is a quarter-mile across the fields, its upper window commanding a clear view of the avenue gate.

turns.narrator: Holmes leads you out through the side door and into the last of the afternoon. Helen watches you go from the threshold, and you do not look back, because looking back would cost her something she has already spent.The path across the fields to the Crown is damp underfoot, the hedgerows throwing long shadows east across the grass. Holmes walks in silence, his chin upon his breast, his hands clasped behind him. You do not interrupt. There is a quality to his silence on the homeward side of a discovery that is different from his silence on the approach: denser, more inhabited, as though he is furnishing a room inside his head that only he can see.The Crown's upper window commands the avenue gate and the inhabited wing beyond it exactly as Helen described. You take the room Holmes has arranged, draw your chairs to the window, and wait. The parish clock marks the quarters. The light fails by degrees over the park wall and the heavy timber of the grounds.Then, at dusk, the sound of wheels on the lane. Roylott's trap passes the gate without pausing, the enormous figure unmistakeable on the box, and turns up the avenue toward the house. Holmes watches until the wheels are swallowed by the dark treeline. Several minutes pass. A light springs up in the sitting-room of the inhabited wing, yellow and steady through the autumn evening.Then the middle window illuminates.Holmes turns from the glass. "She understood," he says.

turns.narrator: Holmes looks at you across the dark window, the middle light of Stoke Moran still burning steadily beyond the glass between you. He does not answer immediately. He has the manner, in this moment, of a man who expected a professional assent and has received something of a different order entirely, something that costs more than professionalism and means more because of it."Then we go," he says. He picks up his cane from the table and tucks it under his arm with the quiet economy of a man who has already made his own preparations and finds yours sufficient. No elaboration. Holmes has never required a man to explain why he stands, only that he does.He turns once more to the window. The light in the middle room burns on, steady and solitary, set there by a woman who repeated the plan back in full and added the final clause herself. She is across the lawn in her old room now, the door locked, the middle bedroom empty above whatever waits inside the iron safe. She has done her part exactly.The light waits; so, now, does Holmes.

choices.text: Go now — cross the lawn before Roylott suspects the window is watched.

Pocket the matches and candle-end Holmes set out — take them yourself.

turns.moment_footnote: The player committed to the vigil through Helen rather than through Holmes — the protection motive, not the professional one. What they are quietly hoping the world noticed is that this was not duty but loyalty, and that the distinction matters. The final line landed as earned clarity rather than mere plot beat. Session 2 should open with Watson already moving, already purposeful, already carrying the weight of what he chose and why — not the weight of what he fears.

turns.narrator: The night air has grown raw with waiting, and your limbs are stiff from the long vigil at the inn window. Across the dark road, beyond the black mass of trees, a single bright light springs out and burns steady in the middle casement of Stoke Moran.Holmes is upon his feet before you have fairly drawn breath. "That is our signal," says Holmes, springing to his feet. "Come, Watson; there is not an instant to lose." At the name you are moving also, for this is no longer a case discussed by lamplight, but a woman shut in with the same danger which killed her sister. The light means that Miss Stoner has done her part. If Roylott has not forestalled us, the window stands ready; if he has, every minute is of consequence, and every sound may be fatal.Across the dark road the middle window burns with a single steady light. Holmes is upon his feet in an instant, and his hand is already on your sleeve. Beyond the trees lies the house where one woman died in terror and another waits this night upon your nerve and his judgment.
